title: Degree-one Reed–Muller functions are affine
statement: Let $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ be a Boolean function lying in the Reed–Muller code $\mathrm{RM}(1,n)$, that is, a function of degree at most $1$. Then $f$ is affine: either $f$ is $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear, meaning $f(x \oplus y) = f(x) \oplus f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \{0,1\}^n$, or the complementary function $x \mapsto \lnot f(x)$ is $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear.
hypotheses_covered: f belongs to RM(1, n), i.e. f is a Boolean function on {0,1}^n of degree at most 1
replaced:
Every $f \in \mathrm{RM}(1, n)$ is affine: either $f$ is $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear or
$\lnot f$ is $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear.
